mainEntity.name: What is exposure bracketing in photography?

acceptedAnswer.text: Exposure bracketing is taking a series of images of the same scene at different exposure values (EV), typically one darker, one brighter, and one near the metered exposure. It helps capture full highlight and shadow detail in high-contrast scenes.

Enable Auto Exposure Bracketing (AEB) or adjust exposure compensation between frames. Choose the number of shots (usually 3–5) and the EV step (±1 to ±3). Use continuous drive so the camera records the sequence quickly and consistently.

mainEntity.name: When should I use exposure bracketing?

acceptedAnswer.text: When scene contrast exceeds the camera’s dynamic range: sunsets/sunrise, backlit subjects, interiors with bright windows, snow/beach scenes, or night cityscapes with deep shadows and bright lights.

mainEntity.name: How many shots and what EV step should I choose?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with 3 shots at ±2 EV for very high contrast, or ±1 EV for moderate contrast. If highlights or shadows still clip, extend to 5 shots or widen the EV step. Check the darkest and brightest histograms to confirm coverage.

mainEntity.name: Do I need special gear for bracketing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most modern cameras support AEB. A tripod improves alignment, but handheld bracketing works in good light. Lock focus and white balance across the series. Shoot RAW at base ISO for maximum editing latitude.

mainEntity.name: What are the benefits of exposure bracketing?

acceptedAnswer.text: It protects important highlights, retains shadow detail, and gives multiple exposure choices. You can select the best single frame or merge the set for a natural-looking HDR with extended tonal range.

mainEntity.name: Are there downsides to exposure bracketing?

acceptedAnswer.text: It increases file count and can introduce ghosting with moving subjects or handheld blur at slow shutters. Merging takes time and care to avoid halos or unnatural tone mapping—use bracketing only when contrast demands it.

mainEntity.name: How do I merge bracketed photos for HDR?

acceptedAnswer.text: Import the RAW set and use HDR Merge in Lightroom or Photoshop. Enable auto-align and de-ghosting if needed. Tone map gently: recover highlights first, lift shadows next, and avoid halos or over-saturation for a natural result.

mainEntity.name: Is bracketing the same as in-camera HDR?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. In-camera HDR blends JPEGs automatically and offers limited control. Bracketing captures separate exposures—ideally RAW—so you can merge later with finer control over alignment, de-ghosting, and tone mapping.

mainEntity.name: What are alternatives to bracketing for high-contrast scenes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Expose to protect highlights and recover shadows from a single RAW, use graduated ND filters to balance sky and land, change composition or timing, add fill light, or rely on computational HDR on smartphones.
